source.title: A Bitter Lesson for Data Filtering
source.authors: Christopher Mohri; John C. Duchi; Tatsunori Hashimoto

record.tranche_reason: The study uses scaling-law projections to estimate when an unfiltered Common Crawl pool could outperform RefinedWeb. It does not test the claim versions about pretraining-loss power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports extensive loss and downstream benchmark comparisons for data-filtering and data-injection conditions. Those experiments address the value of data choices, not whether loss follows the power laws or compute-optimal trends in the claim. The two rows below record its related but distinct projections of the compute needed for an unfiltered pool to beat RefinedWeb.
record.test_reason: The study compares data filters, injected junk data and pool sizes. It uses power-law tools: 6ND compute, power-law fits to decaying loss to extrapolate crossing points (Appendix A.1), and a power law from pool size to a compute target (Figure 6). It never fits or checks loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It does not test compute-optimal allocation, shape effects or downstream predictability. Its 600 tokens/param and 4-epoch allocations are assumptions taken from DeepSeek V4 and Muennighoff et al., not measurements.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that, with enough compute (large models trained long, with epoching), unfiltered Common Crawl beats all tested filters and even benefits from shuffled-word junk data. Their projections put the crossover with RefinedWeb for the 240T-token pool near 1e+30 FLOPs. They add that filtering still matters when compute is the bottleneck.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies data-filtering crossovers rather than reproducing the original loss-scaling-law measurement. Its projections use a 600 tokens/parameter constraint or a four-epoch constraint.
record.method_sensitivity: The projected compute threshold differs between the 600 tokens/parameter and four-epoch assumptions. The paper also reports nonmonotone validation losses at extreme epoch counts.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute needed for the unfiltered CC pool to beat RefinedWeb follows a power law in pool size (linear in log-log, R2 > 0.99). Under two allocation assumptions it projects 3.6e+30 and 9.0e+29 FLOPs for the 240T-token pool. The crossing step count N* grows super-linearly with pool size and shrinks with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute threshold at which unfiltered web data beats filtered data grows as a power law in pool size. Above that threshold, no filtering gives the lowest achievable loss.

record.problems: The compute thresholds are extrapolations from smaller pool-size experiments and depend on assumed allocation constraints. The authors mark extreme-epoch regions as unreliable and report nonmonotone validation losses there.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's many data-filtering, data-injection, and downstream-benchmark comparisons were not included as rows because they address dataset choice rather than the claim versions' loss-scaling or predictability relationships.

untested.parts: No fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Loss curves for 15M–1B models are shown only to compare datasets.
Power-law fits to loss are used only to extrapolate crossing points. Their predictive accuracy for larger runs is not checked.
Compute-optimal N/D allocation is assumed (600 tokens/param or 4 epochs), not measured.
Architecture shapes are fixed per size (Table 2). There is no shape ablation.
There is heavy multi-epoch training and nonmonotone losses at 100+ epochs, but no power-law form is fitted for repeated data.
Appendix B benchmarks (PIQA, ARC-Easy, SocialIQA) compare datasets. No predictive relation to scale or loss is fitted.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices for loss scaling laws.

record.verdict_notes: The record's proposed claim said the threshold scales 'approximately linearly' with pool size. The paper means linear on a log-log plot, i.e. a power law with unstated exponent, so that wording was corrected. Both rows are projections, not measurements, and depend on assumed allocations. The authors mark regions above 121.6 epochs as unreliable.

versions.untested_parts: Whether held-out pretraining loss follows power laws in parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss power laws fitted on small runs predict loss on much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and how either quantity scales with compute.
The effect of depth, width, or other architecture choices at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Whether downstream performance can be predicted from scale or pretraining loss; the appendix reports benchmark comparisons for data-filtering experiments, not a predictive relationship.
Whether the exponents or compute-optimal split in the claim depend on fitting choices or depart from single power laws.

rows.subject: Scaling-law fit (multiple model sizes)
rows.size_stated: 80M, 330M, 1B, and 7B models are shown in the pool-size scaling analysis
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law from pool size to the compute target for the unfiltered pool to outperform RefinedWeb, using a 600 tokens/parameter constraint.
rows.measure: Projected compute threshold for the unfiltered pool to outperform RefinedWeb
rows.note: This is a projection about the data-pool filtering crossover, not a prediction of held-out loss from a loss-scaling law.
rows.check: The row is a projected compute threshold for an unfiltered pool to beat RefinedWeb, not a loss scaling result. 'Observed' has no meaning against any version. The value 3.6e+30 FLOPs is an extrapolation from a power-law fit (R2 > 0.99) over pool sizes up to 10B tokens.
